entries.title: Beyond code generation: A developer’s guide to agentic engineering
entries.summary: Writing code got faster. The work around it didn't. See how you can plan, write code, review changes, and investigate production issues with GitHub Copilot, and what work still needs your judgment. The post Beyond code generation: A developer’s guide to agentic engineering appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
entries.content:
Writing code got faster. The work around it didn’t. See how you can plan, write code, review changes, and investigate production issues with GitHub Copilot, and what work still needs your judgment.

This October, GitHub saw more than 1.2 billion commits in one week—over 400% more than a year earlier. This is more commits than GitHub received in all of 2025. Chances are, you’re generating more code than you were a year ago. But ask yourself: do you feel 400% more productive than you were last year?

Building software takes more than a good prompt. As AI speeds up implementation, software developers are feeling more pressure in other places: a Faros AI study found that pull requests spent 441% longer in review when teams went from low to high AI adoption.

As a software developer, you gather requirements and steer implementation, review changes and evaluate test results, then investigate what happens in production. Agents can help you work more efficiently across all of these stages: Plan, Build, Verify, and Observe. We’ll walk through what an effective agentic engineering workflow looks like on GitHub.

Plan: Get everyone and every agent on the same page

See if this sounds familiar. You’re planning an API change. The design is in one tool, a compatibility requirement is buried in Slack, and an old pull request explains why the current implementation works this way. Before you can write a useful plan, you need to connect those details, compare approaches, and agree on how existing clients will keep working. What looked like a straightforward planning task has become hours of searching, cross-checking, and chasing answers. You’re exhausted before implementation even begins.

You can use Copilot to pull that scattered context into one place, work through the tradeoffs, and turn the decisions into an implementation plan.

  • Plan together where your team already works. Use Copilot in Slack or Teams to collaborate with everyone involved—from product managers and designers to analysts and business stakeholders. Bring in context from connected tools so your team can check assumptions, contribute ideas, and refine requirements together.
  • Turn agreed-upon requirements into actionable work. Ask Copilot to create GitHub Issues with the context and acceptance criteria needed for implementation, breaking out tasks that can be handled separately.
  • Keep routine triage from consuming planning time. Use GitHub Agentic Workflows to label your issues and estimate task complexity. Assign low-complexity tasks directly to Copilot, then spend your time focusing on harder decisions.
  • Give complex work the planning it needs. Use Plan Mode in your preferred Copilot surface to compare approaches and refine an implementation plan. Review and approve the plan before handing it off to Copilot to begin implementation.

What took days of searching and context gathering now produces a reviewable plan, explicit acceptance criteria, and scoped issues, with your time spent on the decisions instead of the retrieval. Then, once you settle on an approach, you’ve already set yourself and your agents up to implement your plan.

Build: Move more than one task forward at a time

You’re ready to turn that plan into code. But life has other ideas. Your agent is halfway through a task, your next meeting starts in five minutes, and your dog has been staring at the door for twenty. Then someone in the meeting points out an edge case the implementation needs to handle. Everyone needs something from you at once. You’d like to keep making progress, but you can’t be in three places at the same time.

You can keep your work moving without being tied to the computer where you started it.

  • Continue your conversation from another device. Session continuity lets you pick up the same Copilot session across clients, so you can work wherever it’s most convenient for you.
  • Let work continue after you close your laptop. Copilot runs tasks in cloud sandboxes, keeping execution off your machine and allowing you to leave and return to a session later.
  • Work on separate tasks without mixing their edits. The Copilot app gives sessions isolated copies of the repository, so an implementation task and a documentation update don’t share an unfinished working tree.
  • Carry project knowledge into each task. Repository instructions capture conventions and validation commands, while shared memory stores useful facts Copilot can reuse across a repository. Copilot Dreaming reviews eligible sessions and pull request feedback to keep memories current and propose instruction or skill updates. That means less time re-explaining how your team works and more consistent help from Copilot across tasks.
  • Match the models to the work. Select Copilot Fusion to choose models and reasoning depth for the task, bringing in additional models to review a solution when needed. You set the effort level to balance quality, cost, and response time.
  • Follow company rules wherever you work. Enterprise managed settings carry your company’s policies and configured tools across Copilot surfaces, reducing setup differences as you move between clients.

Writing code is more than shooting off a single prompt to your LLM and seeing what you get back. And with more work on your plate than ever, it can be difficult to maintain your coding standards and deliver your projects on time. Copilot helps tasks progress independently with shared project knowledge, while letting you pick up a session where you left off across devices. That gives you more room to work through implementation decisions and handle changes as they come up. And as your work finishes, you have focused changes ready to review.

Verify: Spend your attention where it counts

After spending an hour wrangling your agents to get them moving in the right direction, you think you’ve all landed in a good spot. So you open a pull request labeled “small refactor.” It changes 47 files. You wanted feedback on shared validation logic, but it’s buried among updates to every endpoint that calls it, formatting changes, and several hundred lines of generated tests. You wonder how long it will take to get an approval on this, given the endless list of pull requests on your team’s review board.

That review queue is the 441% in practice. You can shorten the wait from both ends: make your changes easier for a person to review, and let Copilot clear the routine checks and fixes before anyone opens the diff.

  • Stack up smaller, more focused pull requests instead of creating a single, massive change. You and your agents can use stacked pull requests to separate dependent work into smaller pieces. This lets each PR be reviewed on its own, keeps dependencies visible, and unblocks teams by letting them build on top of your work before it merges.
  • Catch routine quality issues before they consume review time. GitHub Code Quality checks changes against coding practices and your organization’s standards, catching issues before they reach a human reviewer and saving time for both authors and reviewers.
  • Get review help matched to the change. Copilot code review gives automated feedback, with lighter analysis for simple changes and deeper analysis for complex ones. You can set that depth yourself or let Copilot select it for each pull request.
  • Check security across more of your codebase. AI Scan finds vulnerabilities in languages and files beyond CodeQL’s coverage. AI secret detection helps identify unstructured secrets, such as passwords, that pattern matching can miss.
  • Keep new dependencies within policy. License compliance checks dependency licenses against your company’s rules before merging. GitHub package firewall, currently in public preview for npm, can block downloads that violate configured security policies.
  • Resolve findings and follow-up work without babysitting every pull request. Agentic Autofix proposes repairs for security issues, while Agent Merge automatically addresses failing checks, review comments, and merge conflicts—helping you keep your pull requests moving and preparing them for merge. And, if you configure it, Copilot will even merge your pull requests once your verification steps are passing.

Smaller changes with the routine work already handled means fewer rounds of back-and-forth. Your reviewers get to spend their attention on whether the code does what you intended, and what could go wrong.

Observe: Learn from what happens after you ship

Your change gets approved, the deployment checks pass, and you finally get to cross it off your list. The next morning, your on-call dashboard shows intermittent timeouts, and support reports that a few large customers are affected. Now you’re comparing logs, release history, and customer reports while someone asks whether you should roll back. “All checks passed” feels less reassuring than it did yesterday.

Bring operational evidence and engineering context together so you can decide what to do.

  • Check assumptions against real behavior. With access to your observability tools and business data through connectors such as Fabric, Copilot can help investigate which requests or customer groups are affected.
  • Capture the finding where someone can act on it. Ask Copilot to draft an issue with supporting evidence and acceptance criteria, including a regression test for the failure you uncovered.
  • Carry useful lessons into future work. Review suggested improvements from Dreaming, which uses sessions and repository activity to help refine memories, skills, and code review guidance.

Figuring out what happened after a release can leave you bouncing between dashboards, conversations, and commit history. With Copilot helping connect that information, you can document what you found, create follow-up issues, and improve the guidance available for future tasks. You spend more time deciding what needs to change and less time retracing the investigation. And your next plan starts with what you learned from the software people are actually using.

Where to start

Take one piece of work already on your plate and look beyond the coding task. What context does it need? How will you review and test it? How will you know it worked after it ships?

You don’t have to change your whole process at once. Start with something that frustrates you most this week and put an agent on it. Then expand to other parts of your process over time. Once agents are helping across your whole workflow, you might finally feel as productive as your commit count says you are.

We covered this topic live at GitHub Universe 2026 in “Agentic Engineering: Past the Pilot.”

entries.title: Inside GitHub’s new Git storage architecture
entries.summary: GitHub's new Git storage architecture is built so thousands of agents can push to a single repository at once. Here's how it works. The post Inside GitHub’s new Git storage architecture appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
entries.content:
GitHub’s new Git storage architecture is built so thousands of agents can push to a single repository at once. Here’s how it works.

Last week at GitHub Universe, we announced our new Git storage architecture, capable of handling thousands of writes per second with reads that scale on demand. Through internal testing, we’ve demonstrated the ability to support 5,000 concurrent agents working on a repository, sending 7,200 pushes per second to a repo, all while serving read traffic with consistently low latency. This new architecture is the foundation for GitHub to support agentic development for hundreds of millions of developers, and we’ve been building it underneath GitHub while it keeps running.

Over the past year, agents changed what a busy repository looks like on GitHub. In our first post in this series, we laid out the two principles behind our next-generation Git storage architecture: minimize coordination, and decouple storage from compute. In our last post, we covered the bridge: moving 99.99999% of repositories into Azure, scoping the write quorum to individual references, and standing up virtual replicas backed by Azure Blob Storage.

We also left off with an observation: very little of a write needs to be ordered. Git objects are immutable and named by their contents, meaning two writers can store them at the same time without agreeing on anything. The part of a push that needs agreement is the reference update, and a reference update is tiny in comparison. Virtual replicas were the first step toward building around that, and the means by which we onboard repositories to the new architecture.

The rest of the architecture builds on that observation. Only reference updates need agreement. That lets the parts of Git infrastructure that used to be tightly coupled (storing data, serving requests, and maintaining repositories) scale independently. For developers, Git stays Git: they push, fetch, and branch the same way, with the same protections in place. Below, we walk through the requirements behind the design, follow a request through the system, and dive deep into two of its components.

Building for agent scale

We think about the scale of the GitHub platform along two axes:

  • Horizontal scale is how many developers and agents can work across many repositories. Many of GitHub’s current approaches on this axis have been battle-tested over the years and are carried forward to the new architecture: partitioning of tenants across infrastructure, isolation and/or fairness enforcement of tenant traffic, and load-aware routing, to name a few.
  • Vertical scale is how many developers and agents can work on one repository. As agents write more code, we expect individual repositories to get larger and busier, so most of our requirements came from the vertical axis.

Today, the busiest repositories on GitHub.com receive at most dozens of writes in a single second, typically in short bursts. As more of that work shifts to agents running in parallel and around the clock, we expect those bursts to become a sustained rate within the next year. Each push leads to more reads: CI runs, deployment systems pull the new commit, and other agents fetch it for context. This read fan-out results in a large amplification effect on overall traffic that scales with writes.

We’re already seeing this trend play out on repositories at the top of the curve. The chart below shows daily requests to one repository on GitHub from March to May, when its traffic grew about 4x. Its growth has continued on an exponential trajectory since then.

We have to plan for a world where agent-driven development keeps accelerating at this speed. Instead of planning for the next increment, we set a target of at least two orders of magnitude more scale. For a single repository, that meant the new architecture needed to:

  • Accept thousands of writes per second.
  • Support multiple writer nodes. There are two reasons for this:
    • Experience has taught us that indexing incoming packs and checking object connectivity are the most CPU-expensive parts of a write, and that cost scales with the size of the write, so a single node will become compute-bound quickly.
    • Spreading that work across many nodes improves fault tolerance and shortens recovery when a node fails.
  • Minimize commit latency. An agent waits on each push before it moves to its next step.
  • Record changes in order for each reference with the ability to quickly linearize across references. A virtual replica that falls behind needs to catch up by downloading only the data it needs to serve the incoming request.
  • Keep reads cheap when nothing has changed, which is the common case given the read-to-write ratio.
  • Let each component scale independently.

On top of that, the system had to be able to improve overall reliability and scale globally.

Introducing “Project Rubicon”

In May of 2026, hot on the heels of the initial Azure migration, we started working on a design that could meet those demands. We tried several approaches. In all of them, pack data lived in Azure Blob Storage, and in some we experimented with keeping reference state there too. We’ll cover some of the trade-offs we found below, but we settled on a design we felt maximized throughput while preserving the correctness, durability, availability, and latency guarantees a platform like GitHub requires. We called it “Rubicon,” a nod to the point of no return the industry crossed with agentic development.

Let’s walk through Rubicon from the top down. Many things stay the same: requests from Git clients, the API, and the web UI arrive at Spokes, which still handles routing and load balancing, and serves the internal API that the rest of GitHub uses to read and write repository data. Spokes also maintains its role as a placement and balancing service, maintaining the partitioning, isolation, and tenant fairness required for horizontal scale. The data plane underneath Spokes, in contrast, is new.

Spokes routes each request to one of a small group of virtual replicas assigned to that repository. Virtual replicas are a single fleet of disposable compute that serves reads, writes, or both. A virtual replica’s local disk is a cache that can be rebuilt at any time.

Spokes routes a repository’s traffic to the same virtual replicas when it can, which keeps their caches warm and latency low, but nothing about correctness depends on a request landing on any particular virtual replica. When a virtual replica goes away, the repository’s other virtual replicas keep serving, and a replacement fills its cache as traffic arrives.

When a repository gets busy, we add more virtual replicas. Separately, a fleet of compaction nodes works in the background, directly against Blob Storage and Ref-CAS, to merge each repository’s packs and remove unreachable objects. That work never runs on a virtual replica, meaning their CPU and memory can be almost entirely dedicated to serving requests.

Durable state lives in two places:

  • Git objects, in the form of packs and auxiliary read acceleration data, live in Azure Blob Storage.
  • References and the list of packs that make up the repository (the pack manifest) live in a separate replicated log service we call Ref-CAS (for “Reference Compare-and-Swap”).

Let’s walk the architecture from the perspective of a write and a read:

  • Write: a virtual replica indexes the incoming pack and uploads it to Blob Storage, then commits one transaction to Ref-CAS that lists the pack in the manifest and updates the references. Later, a compaction node merges that pack with others to keep reads fast.
  • Read: a virtual replica checks its reference version with Ref-CAS, pulls the packs it needs from Blob Storage into its cache, and serves the read from there.

There are many distinct approaches we’ve taken within the new architecture, from the software stack on the virtual replicas to how traffic routing and workload scheduling are tuned for different use cases (e.g., many small repos vs. one large one). Let’s dive deep into two components of the architecture and tell their stories centered on the two design principles.

Minimizing coordination: mutating reference state at high throughput

Object storage services like Azure Blob Storage are incredibly good at what they do, and natural fits for many data-heavy applications like source code storage. They are durable and replicated, hold as much as we need them to, have a relatively low cost per byte, and deliver exceptionally high aggregate throughput so long as traffic is spread across many keys. As a result, nearly everything durable in the new Git storage architecture lives in Azure Blob Storage, including:

  • Packs and indexes written by pushes, compaction, and garbage collection.
  • Various read accelerators (like multi-pack indexes, reachability bitmaps, and some custom formats) that our maintenance process builds from those packs.
  • Records that let compaction and garbage collection resume or audit their work, along with the leases that compaction nodes use to claim work.
  • Cached responses for frequently repeated fetches.
  • Checkpoints for the reference state of the repository, though not the authoritative state used to serve requests.

Most of that data is written once to a distinct key and never changes afterward, which is what makes it highly suitable for Blob Storage.

References are the opposite. A busy repository’s references are a relatively small piece of state that many writes race to update at the same time. That access pattern is harder to serve from Blob Storage, and our first prototypes showed us why. Object storage for this kind of workload is an intuitive choice, and one that works well up to a certain level of scale: conditional writes give a compare-and-swap for free, and the data is already durable and replicated. However, we ran into a difficult set of choices, illustrated below by two approaches we tried.

Our first approach was a write-ahead log for all of a repository’s references, indexed by a single blob. Every update is a conditional write against that blob. It’s correct, and reads are cheap: a virtual replica asks whether the blob has changed, and if it hasn’t, it’s done. Writes are where it falls short. Only one conditional write to a blob can be in flight at a time, so even when we batch every push that arrives during a write into the next one, the repository’s write ceiling is one write per round trip to a single blob. In practice, this netted us write throughput in the mid-hundreds per second.

Our second approach split the references across several segment blobs, with each reference hashing to one of them. Writes to references in different segments no longer wait on each other, which raises the ceiling. But a read now has to check every segment to know whether anything changed, and it’s only as fast as the slowest segment. We’d traded write latency for read latency, and reads outnumber writes by orders of magnitude. We can visualize this by showing multiple writes and a read side by side:

Neither option met every requirement, so we built something else: a replicated log service dedicated to references, or the Ref-CAS service. This is the (small) consensus group we said at the end of the last post was still somewhere in the stack. Here’s how it works.

Each reference update in Ref-CAS is a compare-and-swap committed by a quorum. A transaction locks only the references it touches, checks that each one still has the value the writer expects, and becomes visible once a majority of the log’s replicas have recorded it. Agents mostly push to their own branches, so most updates don’t contend, and they replicate in parallel. When two pushes do update the same reference, only one will append to the log.

Each commit to Ref-CAS gets a log sequence number (LSN), and the repository’s version is the LSN of its latest commit. Reads start with a version check against that version. A virtual replica sends the version of the reference state it already holds. If that version is still current, the reply carries no references at all, and an unchanged repository costs a single comparison. If the virtual replica is behind, it gets back the current references and version, along with pointers to pack data and anything else that needs to be known, such as when the last garbage collection cycle occurred.

Unlike the consensus group in our legacy architecture, Ref-CAS never holds or validates object data. It only stores pointers to it. A virtual replica uploads a push’s pack to Blob Storage before it commits the reference transaction. A reference only ever points at objects that are already durable.

These approaches allow us to transact reference state alone in the tens of thousands of operations per second, and provide a baseline for additional annotations on the replication log that help reads decide what to download for a given request.

But supporting thousands of writes per second on a single repository creates a second-order problem: maintaining the performance of reads and writes. For that, we needed a different approach to compaction.

Decoupling storage from compute: compaction at thousands of writes per second

Every push adds a pack to Blob Storage. Git can serve a repository from many packs, but each additional pack makes lookups slightly more expensive, so the pack count can’t grow without bound. In our legacy architecture, compaction runs on the same replicas that serve traffic, and it has to run on every replica. In the new architecture, it runs entirely in the background on separate nodes, directly against durable storage, using the Ref-CAS service to notify virtual replicas of the evolving state.

Compaction nodes each claim ownership over a subset of the repository’s data via a lease, which allows us to scale compaction horizontally. Here’s how one compaction node works through a single shard of a repository’s packs:

The node first takes a lease on the shard in Blob Storage, so only one node compacts a shard at a time. Meanwhile, virtual replicas keep uploading packs and listing them in the pack manifest. The node reads the manifest to find new packs and collects them into an open segment, which is effectively a holding ground for data about to be compacted. When the segment reaches a defined limit based on pack count, size, or age, it seals the segment so it accepts no new packs, then combines its packs into fewer, larger ones. While compaction happens, the next segment for the shard can begin capturing its input packs. Before anything is published, the node checks that the new packs contain exactly the same objects as the inputs. It then uploads the new packs and adds them to the manifest. A second transaction removes the inputs from the manifest, and cleanup deletes them later.

To scale out, this process runs independently for many shards at once. Each pack’s hash maps to a shard, so adding shards and nodes adds compaction throughput. A compacted pack that’s still under the size limit goes back into a shard by its own hash and merges again, so packs grow in tiers until they reach the limit. The net result is an effectively flat pack count while pushes climb:

Compaction merges packs, but it keeps every object. Garbage collection is the step that removes objects nothing references anymore, like the ones left behind by deleted branches and force-pushes. In our new architecture, garbage collection works very similarly to compaction by using dedicated workers to handle the compute-heavy portion. It also has a few special behaviors for safely removing data, which are worthy of their own discussion.

Using these approaches, we’ve been able to consistently demonstrate a flat latency curve as writes climb, and we have other planned optimizations to make the compaction and garbage collection processes themselves more performant.

What comes next

The two principles we started with let each part of this architecture scale on its own. We scale reads and writes by adding virtual replicas. Ref-CAS orders each reference independently instead of the whole repository. We scale maintenance by adding compaction nodes. Our goal is for every repository, from one developer’s side project to the busiest monorepo, to run on the same architecture with no special handling for the busy ones. Repositories don’t stay small. A side project can pick up a fleet of agents overnight, and it shouldn’t need a migration or special handling from us to keep up. One architecture also means every improvement we make reaches every repository at once.

This foundation lets us do a lot more. We’re focused on three areas next: scaling the architecture beyond what we can predict we’ll need today, making agents more efficient at the work they do on GitHub, and evolving Git itself for agentic development.

Improving the architecture

We have plans to take this architecture further. Each of these improvements lets a repository handle more activity while reducing the work behind each request:

  • Read only what’s needed. Fetch a single object from Blob Storage instead of the whole pack that holds it.
  • Organize packs by type. Group commits, trees, and blobs into their own packs. Many requests then touch less data.
  • Partial replicas. Serve requests without every pack on local disk.
  • Materialized views. Keep repository data in ready-to-use forms, like prepared archives, a near-live shallow copy of the default branch, and agent session context stored alongside each commit.
  • Global replicas. Place replicas in any region, close to the workloads that use them. Reads stay within bounded staleness of the latest write.
  • Scale to zero. Grow and shrink the fleet with the repositories that are actually active.

Efficient agent operations on GitHub

Scaling the infrastructure is one side of supporting agents. The other side is making each agent operation cheaper: fewer bytes to fetch, fewer round trips, and less waiting on changes. Each of these fast-follow items builds on the storage work in this post:

  • Work without a clone. Many agent tasks never need a full working tree. They need a handful of files and enough context to make a change. They can read both straight from the server.
  • Atomic commit API. Land a multi-file change in one operation. The whole change commits, or it’s rejected cleanly on conflict.
  • Event streams. Agents and the systems around them work best with real-time information. A generic event stream lets them subscribe to changes and react as they happen.

Improving Git for agents

We also have work to do in Git itself. GitHub has been a longtime contributor to the Git project, and we’re not stopping now. A few examples of the work we’re excited to continue:

  • Lightweight clones. Partial clone, shallow clone, and sparse checkout each let an agent fetch less. Each one has gaps. They don’t always work well together, either. We want to improve each piece and make them fit.
  • Remove hidden scaling costs. Git still has code paths that slow down much faster than the repository grows. Recent releases fixed several of them, but we expect to find more.
  • Faster history walks. Metadata like the commit-graph can answer merge-base and reachability questions without walking every commit. That matters most when an agent’s API call turns into Git work on the server.
  • Avoid common gotchas. Agents make the same mistakes developers do. Git can catch more of the common ones and warn before they cause damage.

Agents have changed how software gets built. GitHub and Git are changing with it. We’re excited to take this new architecture across the starting line. It’s available in a limited private preview now, with a broader rollout early next year. We can’t wait to see what teams build when the number of agents working on a repository is limited by their ideas. We’ll keep evolving Git and GitHub alongside our customers and the Git community.

entries.title: Accessibility statements now have a home on GitHub
entries.summary: GitHub now highlights ACCESSIBILITY.md files and helps maintainers document accessibility goals, known barriers, supported environments, contributor expectations, and reporting processes. The post Accessibility statements now have a home on GitHub appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
entries.content:
Accessibility statements now have a home on GitHub

GitHub now highlights ACCESSIBILITY.md files and helps maintainers document accessibility goals, known barriers, supported environments, contributor expectations, and reporting processes.

Accessibility work often lives in issue trackers, contribution guidelines, audit reports, team knowledge, and conversations with users. When that information has no predictable home, people who encounter a barrier must search for it, and maintainers lose context as contributors and project ownership change.

An ACCESSIBILITY.md file, now visible on repository overview pages, gives a project one durable place to explain its accessibility goals, contributor expectations, supported environments, known limitations, and process for reporting barriers.

GitHub makes accessibility statements easier to find

GitHub now recognizes the ACCESSIBILITY.md file in the repository’s root, .github/ directory, or docs/ directory. A repository can also inherit a statement from its organization’s .github/ repository. For public repositories, maintainers can add or propose a statement from Insights > Community Standards using a concise starter document.

GitHub’s community health files help people understand how a project works:

Contribution guidelines explain how to propose changes

Codes of conduct establish expectations for participation

Security policies explain how to report vulnerabilities

Recognizing ACCESSIBILITY.md gives accessibility information a dedicated place alongside that guidance.

New repositories also include an accessibility issue label by default. The statement explains how to report a barrier and what to expect next, while the label helps maintainers organize and track the resulting work.

Accessibility statements make project practices visible

GitHub CLI’s accessibility statement, for example, documents settings, known barriers, and workarounds. It explains why table output can be difficult to follow with a screen reader and provides a command that prints pull request numbers and titles one per line instead. It also asks contributors changing prompts or output to show the results with relevant accessibility settings enabled. Developers using the CLI get a specific workaround; developers contributing to it get clear expectations for their changes.

The GitHub Annotation Toolkit’s accessibility statement documents a limitation of its Figma library: annotations use canvas position, connecting lines, and matching numbers to visually convey relationships. Access to individual canvas objects does not necessarily communicate what those relationships are.

The statement gives collaborators a concrete alternative: provide a structured text description that identifies each annotated element, its intended semantics and behavior, and any relevant ordering. For developers preparing or receiving a design handoff, this explains what information needs to accompany the visual annotations.

The file also explains how to report accessibility barriers and explicitly states that the library has not undergone keyboard-only or screen-reader testing. Readers get both practical guidance and clear limits on what the project has verified. Showing this information in the repository overview makes it easier to find alongside the project’s other documentation.

Document what the project can maintain

There is no one fixed format for an ACCESSIBILITY.md file. A small library, command-line tool, documentation site, and large web application have different users, risks, and maintenance capacity. Start with accurate information that the project can keep current.

Priorities and goals: Explain why accessibility matters to the project and which user experiences receive attention.

Contributor expectations: Describe the accessibility checks, evidence, or review practices expected for changes, including instructions for human contributors and coding agents.

Reporting accessibility barriers: Provide a direct, accessible reporting path. Do not require disability disclosure, screenshots, or recordings.

Response process: Explain how maintainers acknowledge, triage, track, and communicate about accessibility issues. If the project uses severity levels, let maintainers assign or confirm them during triage.

Supported environments: List the platforms, browsers, input methods, and assistive technologies the project supports or has tested.

Known limitations: Describe barriers in terms of the affected experience, include available workarounds, and link to tracked remediation work.

Ownership and maintenance: Name the team, role, or maintainer responsible for keeping the statement and related practices current.

Feedback and improvements: Explain how users and contributors can suggest changes to the statement or the project’s accessibility practices.

Keep in mind that a project can name a Web Content Accessibility Guidelines version and level as a target. A target does not establish verified conformance. A conformance claim requires an evaluation and should identify the evaluated scope, date, method, and evaluator.

What the most useful ACCESSIBILITY.md files contain

The most useful accessibility statements serve people who arrive after something has already gone wrong. Plain language, descriptive links, and a clear reporting route matter more than legal or standards-heavy language.

Useful reporting guidance invites relevant context, such as the affected task, page, observed behavior, browser, operating system, and assistive technology. It makes screenshots and recordings optional and avoids asking someone to prove a disability.

The statement should also set expectations that maintainers can consistently meet. That can include acknowledgement, status updates, available workarounds, expected timelines, and an opportunity for the reporter to verify a fix.

GitHub’s Community Standards workflow provides a shorter starter with prompts that projects can replace with their own information. The goal is not to produce a perfect policy before publishing the file. Start with accurate information, name the gaps, and update the statement as the project’s accessibility practices mature.

Adding an accessibility statement makes accessibility work more discoverable to users, contributors, and maintainers. Normalizing that practice across open source projects helps make accessibility part of how communities plan, build, report, and improve their work.

Jan Maarten (he/him) is a designer and accessibility specialist living on unceded Duwamish lands. He brings two decades of experience across product design, brand, strategy, and leadership. At GitHub, he bridges design and engineering to improve accessible products, evolve design-system infrastructure, and create resources for the wider design community, including the open-source GitHub Annotation Toolkit.

entries.title: Arnis turns any place on Earth into a Minecraft world
entries.summary: Louis Erbkamm built the first prototype in his free time. Now GitHub Copilot helps him maintain it alone. The post Arnis turns any place on Earth into a Minecraft world appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
entries.content:
Louis Erbkamm built the first prototype in his free time. Now GitHub Copilot helps him maintain it alone.

Louis Erbkamm knows his way around Arnis, the smallest town in Germany, but he’s never set foot in it.

I know where the shops are. Where the boats are… I know the city pretty well, but I haven’t been there yet.

Louis Erbkamm, maintainer of Arnis

Arnis is also the name of his open source project, which takes real-world data from OpenStreetMap and other sources to turn places you know into Minecraft worlds you can freely explore. Since Louis started Arnis in 2022, it’s reached close to 900,000 downloads from GitHub and about 70 contributors.

Two weeks and a slow prototype

Louis grew up playing Minecraft and started coding at 13, always looking for ways to bring code into the game. Arnis began as a fun diversion combining Minecraft with geospatial data, and it went on GitHub, where he already kept his side projects. He finished the first prototype within two weeks while on a break from school.

That first version was Python written by hand, built only on OpenStreetMap, and generating a town took a while. He needed somewhere real to test it, so he looked up towns in Germany, where he lives, and found Arnis. A small town helped while early generation was slow.

Arnis has a lot of buildings, it has streets, it has waters, it has all kinds of different elements that are useful to test with.

Louis

The project didn’t have a name yet, so it borrowed the town’s unique moniker.

A community that brings its own ideas

When Arnis added elevation, its worlds stopped being flat, and geospatial specialists from all over showed up with ideas on how best to integrate it. They started discussions on their own, and Louis says that’s exactly what he needed.

Bigger calls happen in the open too: before porting Arnis from Python to Rust, Louis opened discussions on GitHub to hear different perspectives. Contributors have since translated Arnis into about 20 languages and built major features of their own.

The best thing that has happened to me is essentially this big community on GitHub to see actually people from all kinds of different fields coming together to work on something that I started as a side project.

Louis

How a trash bin gets into Minecraft

Some features start on a walk. Louis noticed how many trash bins there were in his city, and there were none in his generated worlds.

Minecraft has no dedicated bins, so he took the question to the community, and together they found a block that fit. Placing one follows the same path as everything else: for the area a user selects, Arnis queries OpenStreetMap for every mapped element, then looks up each element’s coordinates and type.

If an element isn’t mapped, Arnis can’t place it. For structures too detailed for the map to describe, like the Statue of Liberty in New York, or Christ the Redeemer in Rio de Janeiro, Arnis converts 3D models into Minecraft blocks.

One maintainer, a stack of pull requests

As the sole maintainer, Louis reviews every pull request himself, and they stack up. He usually spends evenings or weekends working on Arnis, which means the community has to wait for him to be done with work for the day.

He uses GitHub Copilot to get an overview of open issues and bugs from the latest release, see how many people are running into them, trace where a bug came from in the codebase, and create a fix. Since he brought AI into the project, he says, code reviews and documentation have both increased.

I could delegate those annoying and boring tasks to Copilot, while I could still have a look at those really cool topics that are related to the development of it.

Louis

Sub-agents that look for regressions

Big features arrive as big pull requests.

Louis opens a large pull request in the GitHub Copilot app for a first overview and a performance review, with Copilot running in the background looking for small changes that would cut memory usage or generation time.

It takes just one wrong calculation in street lights, for example, to make the generation time of an entire city much slower.

Louis

He also keeps a mental list of the areas of the codebase that need extra care whenever someone changes them, and he has written the same warnings out by hand over and over.

I’m starting a few sub agents with the GitHub Copilot app to have a look specifically at those cases, and to come up with corner cases to test to make sure that we do not introduce any regressions into new releases.

Louis

He likes that the terminal, his files, the code changes and the pull request all sit in one app next to the chat.

An unexpected classroom

Louis’s favorite use of Arnis is in schools, where teachers have generated their city or a neighborhood park.

Some turn it into a contest: every student starts from the same generated area, improves a nearby park or playground using Arnis and Minecraft, and the class looks at the results together.

Where Arnis goes next

Recent releases have gone beyond the bounds of Earth, adding the Moon and Mars. Louis wants Arnis to stay easy to use while getting closer to reality, with more detail in less time, and he would like to see it in more schools.

Start with your hometown

Download Arnis from github.com/louis-e/arnis, pick a place on the map, choose where to spawn, and click Start Generation: within a few minutes, the world is ready to open in Minecraft. Louis suggests a place you know, like your hometown or somewhere memorable you’ve been, such as the Grand Canyon or Niagara Falls. Then look for what’s missing.

So maybe you see a bench that was not generated even though it is there.

Louis

Map it on OpenStreetMap, or tell Louis if it’s a bug and he will fix it.
